definition: The point in a planet's or comet's orbit at which it is closest to the sun — the opposite of aphelion, the far point. Though Earth reached perihelion back in January, June invites us to notice that we are now near aphelion, the sun feeling paradoxically close in summer heat yet astronomically distant in orbital fact.
etymology: From Greek peri, meaning near or around, combined with helios, the sun — the same helios who drove his blazing chariot across the sky and gave his name to helium, discovered in the solar spectrum before it was found on Earth. The word entered scientific English in the 17th century as astronomers needed precise language for the elliptical paths Kepler had just described.
usage: A science journalist might write: the comet blazed most brilliantly at perihelion, when the sun's heat vaporized its ancient ices into a tail millions of miles long.
